newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: New Papua New Guinea leader seen as compromise.
newsitem.headline: New Papua New Guinea leader seen as compromise.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's newest leader, John Giheno, is a softly spoken one-time science teacher who plans no major moves in his brief role as caretaker prime minister.

The man charged by the coalition government of this South Pacific nation with restoring stability after the country's worst political crisis in 22 yeas of independence says he is not ambitious and is happy just to serve his country.

Giheno, 47, was sworn in after a day of political negotiating as a temporary replacement for Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan at a simple evening ceremony at Government House, a hilltop colonial building overlooking the sea.

But the non-drinking devout Christian, a Seventh Day Adventist, told reporters he was only filling in and had no major strategy, beyond restoring the troubled capital to normal after the political turmoil of recent days.
"I'm just a caretaker for the time-being. I'm just looking after the job," he said, when asked about his plans as leader.

Chan and two senior ministers, rocked by civil and military opposition, stood aside on Wednesday pending the outcome of an inquiry into a $36 million contract to use mercenaries to quell an island rebellion.
The political crisis saw soldiers lay siege to parliament house, trapping about 100 politicians overnight on Tuesday, and thousands of angry civlians take to the streets.

Giheno, Mining and Petroleum Minister and deputy leader of the Pangu Party, a junior partner in Chan's People's Progress Party-led coalition government, is seen as a competent but not outstanding understudy for Sir Julius, the strongman of PNG's turbulent politics.
"He's a bit of a non-entity," said one Port Moresby political analyst. "He's competent, but would never be a threat to Chan."

Giheno had been regarded a strong chance for the deputy prime minister's job, vacated by Finance Minister Chris Haiveta when he joined Chan in standing aside on Wednesday, pending the outcome of the April 1 to 18 mercenary probe.

He was a surprise choice as Sir Julius' replacement, but appeared to strike a balance between meeting the demands of protesters urging Chan's resignation and Chan's desire to retain a strong influence, the analyst said. "He's a compromise candidate," he added.
Giheno comes from the remote eastern highlands of this rugged and mountainous country and has been a minister for almost all of his 15-year political career.
He has three daughters and a son, with the eldest daughter and son studying in nearby Australia, to the south.
The golf-crazy 14-handicapper says he, like every politician, always dreamed of becoming prime minister, but it was unfortunate to win office this way.
"Well, has ambitions that one day, if the situation is right, that he would get in," he said.
"Unfortunate. Unfortunate it has to come this way."
